chief_complaint: yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week
hpi_details: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he picked up a viral liver infection from contaminated street food he ate during a recent business trip.
concerns: He is worried that his yellow eyes are a sign of aggressive liver cancer and that he will soon be unable to provide for his family.
expectations: He hopes to get urgent blood tests and an abdominal ultrasound to pinpoint what is blocking his liver.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Obstructive Jaundice (Biliary Obstruction) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Obstructive Jaundice (Biliary Obstruction) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes ordering LFTs with fractional bilirubin and an abdominal ultrasound/CT, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week

Key HPI features: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Obstructive Jaundice.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Obstructive Jaundice (Biliary Obstruction).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hepatocellular jaundice (viral or drug-induced hepatitis) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with jaundice — raises concern for ascending cholangitis.
management_principles: Plan for Obstructive Jaundice: Order LFTs, fractional bilirubin, abdominal ultrasound/CT
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of yellow skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools for 1 week. HPI: biliary tract obstruction.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Obstructive Jaundice.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Obstructive Jaundice.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain liver tests with bilirubin fractionation and right-upper-quadrant ultrasound. Use MRCP or EUS when further delineation is needed. Arrange urgent ERCP for ascending cholangitis or selected confirmed obstructing lesions; involve surgery/oncology when imaging suggests malignancy.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Obstructive Jaundice
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Obstructive Jaundice
Implement evidence-based management plan: Order LFTs, fractional bilirubin, abdominal ultrasound/CT. Schedule ERCP

teaching.one_liner: Bile flow from the liver is physically blocked, usually by a stone or tumour, so bilirubin backs up into the blood, turning the skin yellow and the urine dark while stools go pale.
red_flags: Fever with jaundice — raises concern for ascending cholangitis

must_ask.say: Have your stools gone pale, and your urine turned dark, like tea?
Have you had any itching all over your skin?
Do you have any pain in your abdomen, or is the yellowing painless?
Have you had any fevers or shivering?
Have you lost any weight recently, without trying to?
Do you drink alcohol, and are you taking any recently-started medications?

history.answer: My eyes and skin turned yellow about a week ago, and my urine has become very dark while my stools look pale.
It started about seven days ago and has been gradually getting more yellow each day, along with feeling worn out.
Yes, my urine has turned a very dark brownish color, almost like dark tea or cola.
My bowel movements have looked pale and grayish-white, like clay or putty, for the past week.
Yes, my entire body has been terribly itchy for the last few days, especially at night.
I feel a mild, dull ache in my right upper belly, but I haven't had any sharp attacks or sudden cramps after eating.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweats at all.
No, my thinking is completely clear, and I haven't had any unusual drowsiness, easy bruising, or bleeding.
I've been feeling quite tired and sluggish, and my appetite has been a bit lower than usual, but no nausea or vomiting.
No, my weight has been stable, and I haven't noticed any unintentional weight loss.
No, I haven't had any dizziness, lightheadedness, or shortness of breath.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers once or twice a month, and I've never been a heavy drinker.
I'm not taking any prescription medications, herbal remedies, over-the-counter drugs, or health supplements.
No, I haven't eaten any raw shellfish or oysters recently, and no one around me has had yellow eyes or hepatitis.
I don't have chronic hepatitis B or C, never had a blood transfusion, have no tattoos, never used illicit drugs, and have one long-term partner.
No, I've never been told I have gallstones, and I've never had any surgery on my gallbladder or stomach.
No, my stomach hasn't swollen up, and my legs and ankles aren't swollen either.
I've always been healthy and have no history of chronic medical conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
None at all, not even aspirin or vitamins.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I work as an office manager in an accounting firm, and I live at home with my wife.
There is no family history of liver disease, gallbladder problems, jaundice, or gastrointestinal cancers.

I thought maybe I picked up a liver bug or infection from some sketchy street food I ate on a business trip recently. I'm really terrified that turning yellow means I have liver cancer and won't be around to provide for my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert male appearing mildly fatigued with visible generalized jaundice, in no acute distress.
Prominent scleral icterus present bilaterally; conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Generalized yellowish discoloration of the skin with scattered excoriations from scratching; no spider angiomas or palmar erythema.
No flapping tremor or asterixis observed with arms outstretched and wrists dorsiflexed.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no distension, caput medusae, or surgical scars.
Mild deep tenderness in the right upper quadrant without guarding or rigidity; no palpable mass.
Negative Murphy's sign; no inspiratory arrest upon deep palpation of the right upper quadrant.
Liver edge is palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin with smooth contour; spleen is not palpable.
Percussion note is tympanitic throughout; no shifting dullness or fluid wave.
No pitting edema over the pretibial areas or ankles bilaterally.
